The variable aperture lens of the new iPhone 18 Pro is nearly a full stop larger than the fixed aperture lens of the previous generation: jumping from f/1.78 on the iPhone 17 Pro to f/1.48 (the smaller the number, the larger the aperture).

In theory, this change should make the shallow depth-of-field effect more pronounced, with a stronger sense of separation between the subject and the background — but in practice, the difference between the two is quite subtle. In fact, with iPhones from many generations ago, there are already four ways to achieve a shallow depth-of-field effect……

Portrait Mode

The most direct method is, of course, Portrait Mode, which is precisely designed to clearly separate the subject from the background.

This mode works entirely through computational photography (models equipped with LiDAR will use LiDAR to assist) to identify the subject, and then artificially adds blur to the rest. The first generation's effect was quite rough, but in recent years it has become quite excellent.

Macro Photography

The second method is Macro mode, which activates automatically when you are very close to the subject. Once enabled, the iPhone will switch to the ultra-wide lens, which is capable of focusing at extremely close distances.

When using this mode, only a range of a few centimetres can remain sharp, and anything further away will gradually become blurred. As shown in the example below, before taking photos with this mode, be prepared to spend time wiping away dust and cleaning the surroundings! When you see a yellow flower icon appear in the bottom right corner of the frame, it means Macro mode has been activated.

Get Close to the Subject

You can also use the standard lens and get very close to the subject to achieve a similar effect. For example:

Before taking the photo, just tap on the object or person you want to focus on.

Telephoto Lens

The final factor that affects depth of field is focal length. All else being equal, the longer the focal length, the shallower the depth of field, so using the iPhone's telephoto lens can also produce a certain degree of background blur.

Using All Three Methods Together

Using all three methods together yields the best results:

  • Use the telephoto lens
  • Keep the subject as far away from the background as possible
  • Get as close to the subject as possible

When taking portraits, this is the most ideal approach, and it works especially well on the iPhone 15 Pro and later models, because these models are equipped with longer focal lengths.

Conclusion

A larger variable aperture lens is just one of the many new camera features of the iPhone 18 Pro. If you love taking photos, the upgrade is worth it. But if your goal is simply background blur, there are actually other ways to achieve the same effect.
